name: Correct Handling of Stainless-Steel Sheet & Components
desc: Practical handling, storage and contamination-control guidance to protect stainless-steel surfaces before fabrication and delivery.

name: Surface Roughness Basics: Ra, Rz & What a Drawing Is Asking For
desc: A practical introduction to common surface-roughness parameters and why the same Ra value can hide very different surface profiles.

name: How to Use a Vernier Caliper Correctly
desc: A practical guide to external, internal and depth measurement with a vernier or digital caliper, including zero checks, alignment and repeatability.

name: Drawing Revisions: Which Version Goes to the Shop?
desc: A drawing can be dimensionally correct and still be the wrong document. A simple release process keeps quotations, machining, inspection and repeat orders tied to the same approved revision.

name: Choosing a Material Grade for a Replacement Part
desc: Appearance, magnetism and colour can narrow a material search, but they cannot establish a grade. Start with what the part must withstand before choosing a manufacturing route.

name: Shaft, Bearing and Bushing Fits: What to Specify
desc: A fit describes the relationship between two mating sizes. It affects assembly force, running clearance, load transfer and whether a component can be removed for maintenance.

name: Plan the Measurements Before Reverse Engineering
desc: Reverse engineering starts by deciding which features locate, seal, rotate or carry load. Measuring every visible surface with equal priority often misses the relationships that make the part work.

name: Identifying an Unknown Thread Without Guesswork
desc: Thread identification needs more than an approximate outside diameter. Pitch, thread form, taper, handedness and sealing method must agree before two components are considered compatible.

name: Fastener Torque Starts with the Joint
desc: Tightening torque is an indirect way of controlling bolt preload. The joint design, fastener grade, thread condition and friction all affect the result, so one torque value cannot cover every bolt of a given diameter.
keywords: manufacturing fastener torque and joint review

name: Bearing Failure: Preserve the Evidence First
desc: Noise or heat can suggest a bearing problem, but the removed bearing often contains the strongest evidence. Handle it so contamination, wear patterns and lubrication condition remain available for review.

name: Build a Lubrication Plan That Can Be Followed
desc: A useful lubrication plan names the right lubricant, the point of application, the quantity, the interval and the responsible person. “Grease regularly” leaves too much to interpretation.

name: Prepare for Coupling Alignment Before Measuring
desc: Alignment measurements are useful only when the assembly is ready for them. Loose foundations, soft foot, pipe strain or a damaged coupling can undermine a carefully recorded alignment result.

name: Pump Noise: Separate Cavitation from Other Causes
desc: A noisy pump may have suction problems, air ingress, rubbing, bearing damage or an unsuitable duty point. Sound alone cannot confirm cavitation or justify choosing a larger replacement.

name: Hydraulic Hose Replacement: Identify the Whole Assembly
desc: A replacement hose must suit the pressure, fluid, temperature, routing and end connections. Matching its outside appearance leaves important compatibility questions unanswered.

name: Gaskets and Flanges: Specify the Sealing Conditions
desc: A gasket must suit the fluid, temperature, pressure, flange geometry and joint loading. Choosing by outside diameter alone can leave the sealing surface or material unsuitable.

name: Surface Staining or Corrosion? What to Record
desc: Discolouration can come from contamination, surface deposits or active corrosion. Record its location and service conditions before cleaning so that the investigation does not lose useful evidence.

name: Weld Fit-Up: Check the Joint Before Welding
desc: Consistent welding starts with suitable fit-up. Joint access, edge condition, gaps, alignment and fixturing affect whether the planned welding process can produce the required result.

name: Plan for Weld Distortion Before Fabrication
desc: Welding introduces local heating and contraction. A part that looks square in a fixture can move after release, so distortion should be considered while the drawing and assembly sequence can still change.

name: Prepare Artwork for Readable Laser Marking
desc: Good marking starts with a clear artwork file and an agreed marking area. Text height, line width, contrast and the substrate all affect how the final result can be read.

name: Laser Kerf and Small Features: What to Review
desc: The cut has a width, and the material around a small feature must survive the process. Slots, thin webs and tiny holes deserve a review before a drawing is released for laser cutting.
keywords: manufacturing laser cutting kerf and small features

name: Specify the Edge, Not Just “Deburr”
desc: Deburring can mean removing loose material, breaking a sharp edge or producing a controlled radius. The drawing should say which outcome matters without allowing critical geometry to disappear.

name: Press-Brake Tooling: Questions Before Bending
desc: A bend drawing must work with the material and the available tooling. The intended inside radius, flange length and bend sequence can determine whether a part is practical to form.

name: A Fixture Should Locate Before It Clamps
desc: A useful fixture positions the work consistently and holds it without creating avoidable distortion. Start by separating the locating features from the clamping forces.

name: 3D Print Orientation Is a Design Decision
desc: Print orientation affects support marks, surface quality, dimensional behaviour and strength direction. The flattest orientation is not always the best choice for the way a part will be used.

name: Threaded Inserts in Printed Parts: Plan the Boss
desc: Threaded inserts can improve repeated fastening in suitable printed polymers, but the surrounding boss and installation process still control the result.
keywords: design threaded inserts in printed parts

name: Prototype Validation: Decide What You Are Testing
desc: A prototype is most useful when it answers a specific question. Appearance, assembly fit, ergonomics and load performance may require different materials, processes and inspection methods.

name: First Article Inspection: Agree the Plan First
desc: First Article Inspection checks whether the first representative output meets the agreed requirements. It works best when the drawing, characteristics, methods and evidence are defined before the part arrives.

name: Measurement Uncertainty: Leave Room for Doubt
desc: A measurement is an estimate made with an instrument and a method. Resolution, calibration, temperature, contact and repeatability influence how confidently a result can be compared with a tolerance.

name: Turn a Drawing into an Inspection Plan
desc: An inspection plan connects each requirement with a method, a frequency, a record and an acceptance decision. It makes the drawing usable by the people checking the output.

name: Choose a Surface Finish for Its Job
desc: A finish can serve appearance, sliding contact, corrosion control, cleaning or sealing. These needs should be separated before a supplier is asked for a polished or premium surface.

name: Replacement Parts: Plan the Trial Fit
desc: A replacement should be checked in its assembly context, particularly when the original geometry or tolerance was uncertain. A planned trial fit is more informative than discovering interference during urgent commissioning.

name: Packing Precision Parts for Transport
desc: A part can pass inspection and arrive damaged. Packaging should protect the features that control fit, appearance and cleanliness, while preserving the records needed to identify the shipment.

name: Maintenance Handover: What Must Be Recorded
desc: A maintenance job is not complete when the tools are removed. The receiving team needs to know what was found, what changed, what was verified and which restrictions or follow-up actions remain.

name: Critical Spares: Stock the Risk, Not Every Part
desc: A useful spares plan considers failure consequence, replacement lead time, interchangeability and storage life. Stocking everything is expensive, while stocking familiar low-risk parts can leave the real bottleneck uncovered.

name: A Bill of Materials That Matches the Assembly
desc: A bill of materials links an assembly to the parts, quantities, specifications and revisions needed to build it. It should describe the released configuration rather than a convenient list copied from an old quotation.

name: Piping Layout Review Beyond the Centreline
desc: A piping layout must accommodate operation, support, drainage, maintenance and installation as well as the nominal route. The centreline alone does not show whether a system can be built and serviced.
